plan: Complete enhanced-ACT passage set: one original natural science passage of about 600 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000031) on urban heat islands (causes, unequal effects, reflective roofs, street trees), with 9 questions (Key Ideas and Details 3, Craft and Structure 4, Integration 2). Factual claims kept to well-established points (night-time peak, heat storage by paved surfaces, evaporative cooling by vegetation, climate-dependent effect of reflective roofs).

passages.title: The Island in the City
passages.text:
On a still summer evening, a thermometer in the center of a large city may read several degrees higher than one in the farmland a few miles away. The difference is not a quirk of a single instrument. Measured across many cities and many years, the pattern is consistent enough to have a name, the urban heat island, and it is usually strongest not in the afternoon, when the sun is high, but after dark. In a large city on a calm, clear night, the gap between downtown and the surrounding countryside can be considerably larger than it is at midday, and it tends to shrink when clouds or a strong wind move in.

That timing is a clue to the cause. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them and store the energy as heat. A field of grass or a stand of trees absorbs sunlight too, but plants also release water vapor through their leaves, and turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air. A city has replaced much of that cooling vegetation with materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by trapping some of the heat that the streets radiate upward, and engines, air conditioners, and furnaces add heat of their own.

The consequences are not evenly shared. Within a single city, temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next, and the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement. Because heat that lingers into the night denies the body a chance to recover, these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave, especially for older residents and for people without air conditioning.

One response has been to make surfaces reflect more sunlight. A roof coated in a pale, reflective material can stay far cooler on a sunny afternoon than a dark one, and some cities now require or encourage such roofs on new buildings. The idea is simple, but its effects depend on circumstances. In a place with hot summers and mild winters, a reflective roof saves energy that would have gone to cooling. In a place with long, cold winters, the same roof also reflects sunlight that would have helped warm the building, and part of the summer savings may be lost.

Trees offer a different kind of help. A street tree shades the pavement beneath it, so less sunlight is stored in the first place, and it cools the air through its leaves. Unlike a coating, though, a tree takes years to grow, needs water and room for its roots, and can be lost to drought or disease. Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees. Many cities now try to do both.

Researchers continue to argue about how much each measure can accomplish, and the answer clearly varies from city to city. What is no longer in dispute is the basic picture: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it, which means that it can also be changed by the choices made in rebuilding it.

candidates.subskill: Central idea of an informational passage
candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Cities are warmest in the afternoon because their buildings block cooling winds.
choices.B: Reflective roofs are the most effective way to cool a city in any climate.
choices.C: Cities are warmer partly because of how they are built, and rebuilding can reduce that.
choices.D: Older residents face greater risks than other people during long summer heat waves.

candidates.evidence: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it
candidates.explanation: The passage explains why cities are warmer, who is affected, and how coatings and trees can help, ending with the point that building choices make cities warmer and rebuilding choices can change that.

A.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the effect is strongest after dark, and wind is not discussed.

B.rationale: Paragraph 4 says reflective roofs' effects depend on the climate.

D.rationale: This is a detail from paragraph 3, not the main idea.

hints: Which choice covers the causes and the responses?
candidates.remember: A main idea must cover the whole passage.

candidates.subskill: Inference about timing from a cause
candidates.stem: Based on paragraphs 1 and 2, the urban heat island is usually strongest after dark mainly because:

choices.A: city materials that stored heat during the day give it back slowly at night.
choices.B: the sun is high in the sky during the late afternoon and early evening.
choices.C: plants release more water vapor at night than during the day.
choices.D: people use more air conditioners at night than in the afternoon.

candidates.evidence: materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 notes the effect peaks after dark, and paragraph 2 explains that city materials store heat all day and release it slowly through the night.

B.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the effect is strongest after the high-sun hours, not during them.

C.rationale: The passage does not compare plants' release of water vapor by time of day.

D.rationale: Waste heat is mentioned only as an added factor, with no comparison by time of day.

hints: Paragraph 2 calls the timing 'a clue.' What does it point to?

strategy.explanation: Connect the timing in paragraph 1 to the cause in paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: Link a pattern in one paragraph to its explanation in the next.

candidates.stem: The author mentions that plants release water vapor through their leaves (paragraph 2) mainly to:

choices.A: show that plants absorb less sunlight than asphalt and brick do.
choices.B: suggest that cities should water their lawns and parks more often.
choices.C: introduce the health risks that heat brings to older residents.
choices.D: help explain why replacing vegetation with pavement makes a city warmer.

candidates.evidence: turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air
candidates.explanation: The detail explains how vegetation cools the air, so replacing it with heat-storing materials removes that cooling and helps make the city warmer.

A.rationale: The passage says plants absorb sunlight too; the point is their cooling, not their absorption.

C.rationale: Health risks come in paragraph 3 and are not linked to water vapor.

hints: What does the city replace plants with?

strategy.explanation: Ask why the detail sits in a paragraph about causes.

candidates.remember: A detail usually supports the paragraph's main point.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word carry most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave
candidates.explanation: Blocks that 'carry real risks' present or pose those risks to their residents.

A.rationale: This is the common meaning, but nothing is being moved.

C.rationale: This would mean holding up a weight, which does not fit risks.

D.rationale: This sense, as in carrying an election, does not fit risks.

hints: Try each choice in the sentence.

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own, then match.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the sentence, not the most common one.

candidates.subskill: Applying the passage to a new case
candidates.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following places would most likely be the hottest on a summer night?

choices.A: A neighborhood near the city center with wide streets lined by large trees
choices.B: A neighborhood at the edge of the city next to open farmland
choices.C: A block of apartments surrounded by parking lots and almost no trees
choices.D: A large park with a broad lawn, a pond, and scattered shade trees

candidates.evidence: the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the hottest blocks have the fewest trees and the most pavement, and paragraph 2 explains that pavement stores heat and releases it at night.

A.rationale: Trees shade pavement and cool the air, which lowers night heat.

B.rationale: Paragraph 1 says areas near farmland are cooler than the city center.

D.rationale: Vegetation cools the air, so a park would be cooler.

hints: Which features does paragraph 3 link to the hottest blocks?

strategy.explanation: Apply the passage's causes to each choice.

candidates.remember: Apply the author's stated causes to a new example.

candidates.subskill: Applying a qualified claim to choose a setting
candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 4, in which of the following places would a reflective roof most likely produce the greatest net energy savings over a year?

choices.A: A town with long, hot summers and short, mild winters
choices.B: A town with short, cool summers and long, cold winters
choices.C: A town with mild summers and mild winters but very little sunshine
choices.D: A town with hot summers and long, cold winters with deep snow

candidates.evidence: In a place with hot summers and mild winters, a reflective roof saves energy that would have gone to cooling.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says reflective roofs save cooling energy in hot summers but lose some of those savings in long, cold winters, so the best case has long hot summers and mild winters.

B.rationale: A reflective roof here would also block winter sunlight that helps heat buildings.

C.rationale: With little sunshine, a reflective roof has little sunlight to reflect.

D.rationale: Long, cold winters would cancel part of the summer savings.

hints: What does a reflective roof do in summer and in winter?

strategy.explanation: Weigh the summer gain against the winter loss for each choice.

candidates.remember: Weigh both sides of a trade-off the author describes.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must weigh a summer benefit against a winter cost; the choice with hot summers but long winters is a strong trap.

candidates.subskill: Author's view of a proposed solution
candidates.stem: The author's view of reflective roofs is best described as which of the following?

choices.A: They waste energy in every climate and should not be required.
choices.B: They work better than street trees in every city that uses them.
choices.C: They save more energy in cold climates than in warm climates.
choices.D: They can save energy, but how much depends on the local climate.

candidates.evidence: The idea is simple, but its effects depend on circumstances.
candidates.explanation: The author presents reflective roofs as useful but says their effects depend on circumstances, especially winter length.

A.rationale: The author says they save energy where summers are hot and winters mild.

B.rationale: The author never ranks roofs above trees, and says results vary.

C.rationale: This reverses the author's claim about cold winters.

hints: What qualification does the author add after describing the roofs?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence that begins 'The idea is simple.'

candidates.remember: Look for the author's qualification, not just the description.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 5, planners who think in decades most likely favor trees because they believe that:

choices.A: trees cost much less to plant than the coatings that are applied to roofs.
choices.B: over many years, a tree's slow start matters less than its two benefits.
choices.C: coatings cannot be applied to buildings that have already been built.
choices.D: trees, unlike roof coatings, can never be lost to drought or disease.

candidates.evidence: Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 lists a tree's two benefits (shade and cooling) and its main drawback (it takes years to grow). Over decades the slow start matters less, so long-range planners favor trees.

D.rationale: Paragraph 5 says trees can be lost to drought or disease.

hints: What is the drawback of trees, and why would it matter less over decades?

strategy.explanation: Contrast quick results with a long time span.

candidates.remember: A drawback that is about time matters less over a long period.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must infer the planners' reasoning from the contrast between quick results and decades; out-of-scope cost and feasibility claims are tempting.

candidates.stem: The last paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: acknowledge an ongoing debate while stating what is no longer disputed.
choices.B: introduce a new way of cooling cities that the passage has not yet described.
choices.C: argue that reflective coatings should replace street trees in most cities.
choices.D: summarize the health risks of heat for older residents and others.

candidates.evidence: What is no longer in dispute is the basic picture
candidates.explanation: The paragraph notes that researchers still argue about how much each measure helps, then states the undisputed point that building choices affect a city's temperature.

B.rationale: No new method appears in the last paragraph.

C.rationale: The author never argues for replacing trees.

D.rationale: The health risks appear only in paragraph 3.

hints: What does the paragraph say is disputed, and what is not?

strategy.explanation: Look for the contrast in the paragraph.

candidates.remember: A closing paragraph often separates what is settled from what is not.
